transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-28T14:30:00Z
Duration: 56 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Alice Morgan (Redwood AE), Ben Cho (Redwood SE), Maya Patel (Head of ML, Ember), Raj Singh (CTO), Samir Rao (Infra), Olivia (PM)

Summary:
- Ember is evaluating migrating generation workloads from OpenAI-hosted to Redwood Dedicated (possible Private later) to reduce unit cost and gain throughput/observability.
- Main concerns: API compatibility (tool-calls, streaming), eval parity (same generations quality), infra/ops (KV cache, batching, vLLM/TGI compatibility), and security/compliance (SOC2, SSO, KMS).
- Agreed next steps: security pack, benchmark run with Ember prompts, pricing options, and small pilot on Dedicated.

Topics covered:
- Current stack and pain points
- Model compatibility and eval parity
- Performance (latency, throughput, batching) and host vs dedicated tradeoffs
- Security, networking (VPC), KMS, SSO
- Pilot scope and timeline

00:00 - Alice Morgan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Alice, AE on the account, and with me is Ben our solutions engineer. How's everyone doin?
00:12 - Maya Patel: Hey Alice, good, thanks. We were hoping to dig into how Redwood Dedicated would map from our current OpenAI usage.
00:20 - Raj Singh: Yep, mostly cost and predictable latency; also we want to keep tool calling and streaming intact because product depends on it.
00:30 - Ben Cho: Great, will do a mix of architecture and technical detail. Quick qual q's: what is your current qps/throughput, average seq length and model family?
00:45 - Maya Patel: Right now on OpenAI we see bursts up to 120 rps, avg sequence length about 700 tokens for our long-form summarization and conversational flows. Cost is getting up there, and we're also seeing occasional throttling during peaks.
01:05 - Samir Rao: Plus we want more visibility into token-level cost breakdowns and latencies - our finance and platform teams keep asking.
01:15 - Ben Cho: Okay, that helps. On the model side, are you using gpt-4o-style or 3.x, and any fine-tuned weights?
01:25 - Maya Patel: We're on mix - some gpt-4 families for high-value flows, but we also have a few in-house fine-tuned models hosted on OpenAI for domain adapt. We run a reranking step with embeddings too.
01:40 - Alice Morgan: Good context. From Redwood's side, Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools, predictable throughput and can host the model variants you need. We support API-compatible endpoints and have a mapping layer for OpenAI-style requests. That said, there are a few gap notes around some tool-calling edge cases; Ben will cover those.
02:05 - Ben Cho: On compatibility: we try to be API-first. Most normal text generation, streaming, and function-calling flows map directly. For advanced tool-calling with nested function schemas there's occasionally schema validation differences; we recommend a quick smoke test. Also note: if you're using OpenAI fine-tunes, we can run inference on exported model artifacts or reconfigure on our runtime, but the process varies per model.
02:40 - Raj Singh: Quick question - we evaluated self-hosted vLLM/TGI earlier. How does Redwood Dedicated compare to running vLLM on our infra? Cost-wise and ops-wise?
03:00 - Ben Cho: Good one. Fragmented answers: if you run vLLM yourself, you get full control but significant ops overhead (build, kernel tuning, autoscaling, fallback). Redwood Dedicated removes that ops burden and gives performance optimizations (kernel selection, batching, KV-cache management) that are tuned per-model. For cost per-token, with committed Reserved Capacity we can often beat raw cloud infra once you factor engineering time and reliability. But we shouldn't oversell — there are cases where certain custom kernels in vLLM may be marginally faster for niche models.
03:36 - Maya Patel: And eval parity — we need the outputs to match our current OpenAI baselines. Any variance is a blocker.
03:45 - Ben Cho: Understood. We do eval parity work routinely. We recommend you share a representative eval set; our Optimize team will run A/B comparisons across model variants and quantization profiles. We also run temperature/sampling parity tests. Expect small differences due to tokenization and backend variants; we focus on functional parity (rankings, major intents) rather than bit-for-bit equality.
04:10 - Olivia (PM): Will devs need to change prompt engineering or code?
04:18 - Ben Cho: Minimal. We provide an API mapping for OpenAI calls; minor changes might be required for certain client libraries. For streaming and tool-calls, the semantics are preserved but we advise a small compatibility shim for retries and webhook handling.
04:40 - Samir Rao: Network/topology: we need VPC peering or Private deployment. Ember operates in a locked-down VPC and we have strict egress rules. Can Dedicated be VPC-connected or do we need Redwood Private?
04:55 - Alice Morgan: Good question. Dedicated can be provisioned with private networking options — we offer VPC attachments for Dedicated clusters in supported regions. If you need a customer-managed control plane or on-prem air-gap, that's our Private product which is a larger engagement. For now, Dedicated with VPC peering is a common middle ground.
05:20 - Raj Singh: KMS and key management? Encryption at rest and in transit?
05:26 - Ben Cho: We integrate with customer KMS (AWS KMS, GCP KMS) for encryption at rest and have TLS for in-transit. For Private we can support HSM. We'll include our KMS integration docs in the security pack we'll send.
05:40 - Maya Patel: Compliance: SOC2, and we need audit logs for tokens and model versions — do you provide that?
05:48 - Alice Morgan: Yes, we provide audit logging, model version lineage, and can include per-route logs with retention options as an add-on. SOC2 Type II report and ISO artifacts will be included in the security pack.
06:05 - Ben Cho: Regarding performance: based on 120 rps bursts and 700 token average, we'll propose a Dedicated config with autoscale headroom for 150 rps sustained bursts, and caching for prefix responses to cut costs. Our batching and KV cache can reduce per-token compute. We'll show modeled unit economics in the pricing pack.
06:30 - Raj Singh: How do quantized models affect eval parity? We looked into 4-bit quant and saw scoring drop in some edge cases.
06:40 - Ben Cho: Right. Quantization can introduce subtle changes. Our Optimize team runs quantization profiles per-model and per-workload and flags regression risks. For critical flows we recommend using higher precision or running a canary: serve small percentage on higher precision and run metrics. We also support hybrid strategies (hot paths in FP16, bulk generation in 4-bit).
07:05 - Maya Patel: On tooling: can we run our eval harness (pytest-style suite) against Dedicated?
07:12 - Ben Cho: Absolutely. We'll provision a test endpoint and run your harness as part of the benchmark. We usually run side-by-side A/B with OpenAI baseline and produce metrics: token-level latency, P95, failure modes, and quality metrics (BLEU/ROUGE/embedding similarity/rerank parity).
07:35 - Olivia: About pricing — we need both per-token hosted and reserved options in one doc. Also want an estimate for a 3 month pilot.
07:45 - Alice Morgan: We'll include three commit tiers and a pilot estimate. Pilot often is 1-2 Dedicated nodes with a short-term commit or trial credits. We'll outline upgrade paths to Private if you need.
08:00 - Samir Rao: Any downtime risk during migration? We need rollback strategies.
08:08 - Ben Cho: We'll advise a canary rollout, traffic split, and automatic fallback to OpenAI if latency/quality thresholds aren't met. Redwood supports model routing policies and automatic fallback to hosted variants.
08:25 - Raj Singh: Security review: legal will want to see data handling, retention, and logging. Does Redwood allow us to control retention windows?
08:35 - Alice Morgan: Yes, retention policies are configurable per-route and we can turn off retention for sensitive data. We'll send the legal/security FAQ.
08:45 - Maya Patel: One more — do you support embeddings and vector stores, or do we need separate infra?
08:52 - Ben Cho: We support embeddings generation; Redwood doesn't host a managed vector DB by default but we integrate with common vector stores and provide export hooks. For reranking we can do in-line embedding calls and give exports.
09:05 - Maya Patel: Cool. For the benchmark, what's the expected timeline?
09:10 - Ben Cho: If you share the eval set by 2026-05-03, we can run benchmark and share results by 2026-05-08. Requires about 2-3 days of tuning if quantization tradeoffs are explored.
09:25 - Alice Morgan: Recap of ask: Ember will share sample prompts and logs. Redwood to send security pack and pricing, Ben will prepare benchmark harness. We propose a pilot for early May.
09:40 - Raj Singh: Who will own the pilot infra? We want to ensure our infra team can approve VPC peering.
09:46 - Alice Morgan: We'll coordinate with Samir to scope the VPC peering steps. Ben will include an ops checklist.
10:00 - Olivia: Any blockers on legal for NDA?
10:05 - Alice Morgan: We can send a standard mutual NDA; if you need custom terms we'll escalate.
10:12 - Samir Rao: Minor nit: we saw some references to Redis-like KV cache in docs; is that something we manage?
10:20 - Ben Cho: The KV cache is managed within Redwood runtime; for Private or certain Dedicated configs we can expose cache metrics and optional control plane hooks, but it's managed to keep latency guarantees.
10:35 - Maya Patel: Great. On the integration path, what sample code do you provide?
10:40 - Alice Morgan: We'll attach our API compatibility doc and SDK snippets for Node/Python plus a migration guide. The doc will include common mapping patterns from OpenAI to Redwood endpoints.
10:50 - Raj Singh: Also, we're running TGI on some experimental flows. Is that compatible?
10:56 - Ben Cho: Yes, for the most part. Redwood supports model variants that are TGI-compatible; the key is the model artifact format. We'll validate artifacts during onboarding.
11:10 - Maya Patel: Any rough numbers on latency P95 for a 700-token request on Dedicated?
11:18 - Ben Cho: Ballpark: depending on model family, optimized runtime, and batching, P95 could be 600-1100 ms for a 700-token generation on GPU-optimized stacks — with dedicated GPUs and correct batching. We'll confirm after a quick perf run.
11:36 - Alice Morgan: Ok wrapping up, thanks everyone. We'll send the docs and set up the benchmark slot.
11:45 - Maya Patel: Thanks, appreciate it.
11:50 - Raj Singh: Thanks all.

Action items (explicit in call):
- Alice Morgan to send security pack (SOC2, ISO artifacts, KMS details) by 2026-04-30.
- Ben Cho to prepare benchmark plan and provisional dedicated config by 2026-05-01.
- Maya Patel to share eval prompt set and sample logs by 2026-05-03.

End of transcript.
